The Education

Why GI Billing Loses More Revenue Per Procedure Than Any Other Specialty

The screening-to-therapeutic colonoscopy conversion is the single highest-dollar per-claim coding error in U.S. outpatient medicine. PMEx eliminates it systematically.

Gastroenterology billing is the process of coding and submitting insurance claims for diagnostic and therapeutic GI endoscopy, inflammatory bowel disease management, hepatology services, and the infusion and injection services that accompany biologic treatment programs. The U.S. GI market generates over $40 billion in annual procedure revenue and the billing complexity is proportional to that scale.

The most consequential coding decision in gastroenterology is the screening vs. diagnostic colonoscopy distinction and within that, whether a screening colonoscopy that converts to therapeutic mid-procedure should be billed with the original screening modifier or with the appropriate therapeutic code. A screening colonoscopy (G0121 for Medicare, 45378 with modifier 33 for commercial) becomes a therapeutic colonoscopy the moment a polyp is removed, a biopsy is taken, or a treatment is applied. The difference in reimbursement between screening and therapeutic coding on a colonoscopy with polypectomy is $400 to $600 per procedure. Applied incorrectly across 15 procedures per day, that is $6,000 to $9,000 daily in incorrect billing.

Biologic prior authorization for IBD is the second major revenue management challenge. When a Crohn's or ulcerative colitis patient requires adalimumab, infliximab, vedolizumab, or ustekinumab, most commercial payers require step therapy documentation (trials of conventional therapy), clinical evidence, and specific disease severity markers before approving treatment. Managing this authorization for dozens of active IBD patients simultaneously, while tracking renewal cycles every 6 to 12 months, requires a dedicated workflow that most GI billing teams do not have the infrastructure to run correctly.

The GI billing opportunity most practices miss:

Correctly coding every screening colonoscopy that converts to therapeutic during the procedure recovers $400 to $600 per case. For a 3-provider GI group performing 25 scopes per day, the annual recovery from conversion coding alone exceeds $1.5 million in correctly submitted claims.

The Biggest Coding Error in U.S. GI Billing

The Colonoscopy Screening-to-Therapeutic Conversion Trap

A screening colonoscopy scheduled as a preventive service (G0121 for Medicare, 45378 with modifier 33 for commercial payers) converts to a therapeutic procedure the moment a polyp is removed, a biopsy is taken, or any treatment is applied. That conversion determines both the correct CPT code and the patient's financial responsibility and getting it wrong costs the practice $400 to $600 per procedure while simultaneously creating a surprise bill for a patient who expected a zero-cost-sharing screening visit.

The conversion rule: when a screening colonoscopy becomes therapeutic, the appropriate therapeutic CPT code applies 45385 for polypectomy via snare, 45380 for biopsy, 45384 for cold forceps polypectomy. These codes reimburse significantly higher than the screening code. Many GI billing teams submit the therapeutic code but forget to apply the correct preventive modifier, causing the patient to incorrectly receive a cost-sharing obligation for what started as a screening visit. Others bill the screening code even after polyp removal, leaving the therapeutic reimbursement uncaptured.

PMEx tracks the procedure documentation from the endoscopy report, identifies conversion events, applies the correct therapeutic CPT with the appropriate preventive modifier for each payer, and manages patient notification about any cost-sharing changes. No conversion case is coded incorrectly. No patient receives a wrong cost-sharing bill.

WRONG CODE

Screening Code Applied After Polyp Removal

Colonoscopy scheduled as screening. Polyp found and removed via snare. Billed as G0121 (screening) instead of 45385 (polypectomy). Practice receives $180 instead of $580. $400 per procedure lost permanently. At 10 polypectomies per day, that is $1.4 million annually in underbilling.

WRONG MODIFIER

Therapeutic Code Without Preventive Modifier

Correct therapeutic CPT (45385) applied after polypectomy. Preventive modifier dropped. Patient receives full cost-sharing bill for what they scheduled as a zero-cost screening. Patient disputes. Practice spends hours resolving billing complaints that correct coding would have prevented.

PMEX CORRECT

Therapeutic Code + Correct Preventive Modifier + Patient Notification

PMEx reads the endoscopy report, identifies the conversion event, applies 45385 with the correct preventive modifier per payer-specific rules, and submits the claim for full therapeutic reimbursement with correct patient cost-sharing applied. No coding error. No billing surprise. Full revenue captured on every procedure.

IBD Drug Administered Without Active Authorization

Infliximab infusion administered. Authorization expired 3 days prior. Renewal request submitted late. Payer denies the $8,000 drug administration claim retroactively. Patient's treatment is already complete.

ERCP Add-On Code Error

ERCP Add-On Procedures Not Separately Billed

ERCP performed with sphincterotomy, stone extraction, and stent placement. Primary ERCP code submitted alone. Sphincterotomy (43262), stone extraction (43264), and stent placement (43274) add-on codes never applied. $1,200 to $2,400 per ERCP left uncaptured.

PMEx reviews the endoscopy report for every ERCP procedure and identifies all separately billable add-on components. Full ERCP code set applied primary plus all applicable add-ons before submission.

AEC Facility Billing Error

Wrong POS or Missing Facility Claim

Procedure performed at freestanding AEC. Professional claim submitted correctly. Facility claim never submitted. Or both professional and facility claims submitted with wrong POS code. $800 to $2,000 in facility revenue per procedure permanently lost.

PMEx manages AEC facility billing as a parallel workflow to professional claims correct POS, separate facility CPT and HCPCS codes, and payer enrollment specific to freestanding AECs. Professional and facility revenue captured on every endoscopy case.

Medical Necessity Denial

Colonoscopy Surveillance Interval Not Documented

Patient returns for surveillance colonoscopy at 3-year interval. Commercial payer requires documented clinical justification for the surveillance interval selection. Without specific polyp histology from prior scope, payer denies as routine screening patient owes deductible; practice gets screening reimbursement.

PMEx reviews prior colonoscopy documentation to confirm appropriate surveillance interval is documented before claims for follow-up scopes are submitted. Clinical justification confirmed in the note, correct code applied, correct cost-sharing communicated to patient.

Infusion Hierarchy Error

Biologic Infusion Hierarchy Billed Incorrectly

IBD patient receives infliximab infusion (J1745) plus iron infusion (J1756) in the same session. Primary infusion code applied to the iron infusion (lower value) instead of the infliximab (higher hierarchy drug). Infusion hierarchy rules require the highest-value drug as the primary code. Revenue impact: $200 to $400 per dual-infusion session.

PMEx applies CMS infusion hierarchy rules to every dual-drug infusion session selecting the primary infusion code based on drug hierarchy, applying sequential add-on codes correctly. Correct infusion hierarchy on every session, every drug combination.
